We moved DNS providers on Monday. Since then some users get SERVFAIL for example.com and others are fine. Output:

$ dig +dnssec example.com A
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: SERVFAIL

$ dig example.com DS
;; ANSWER: example.com. 3600 IN DS 2371 8 2 4F3AC91B...

$ dig example.com DNSKEY
;; ANSWER: example.com. 300 IN DNSKEY 257 3 8 AwEAAc9... (key tag 58114)

The two halves of DNSSEC no longer match. The parent zone still publishes a DS record for key tag 2371 (the old provider's key), while your new zone is signed with key tag 58114. A validating resolver builds the chain, finds no DNSKEY matching the DS, and declares the zone bogus - that is exactly what SERVFAIL means here.

That also explains "some users": resolvers that validate (Google, Cloudflare, most ISPs) fail; resolvers that don't validate return the records happily.

Fix at the registrar (where the DS lives, not at the DNS provider): replace the DS record with one computed from the new provider's DNSKEY, or delete the DS entirely to run unsigned until the new DS is ready. Then wait for the parent-zone TTL and confirm with `dig +dnssec example.com` - you want status NOERROR and the `ad` flag set.

Laptops on our VPN intermittently fail to resolve git.corp.internal. Sometimes it works for an hour, then NXDOMAIN. A laptop's resolv.conf:

nameserver 10.0.0.2
nameserver 8.8.8.8

dig @10.0.0.2 git.corp.internal returns 10.0.4.17 every time. dig @8.8.8.8 returns NXDOMAIN.

The bug is having both of those nameservers in one list. A stub resolver does not know that 10.0.0.2 is "for internal names" - it treats the list as interchangeable servers for everything, and it will switch between them on timeouts, slow answers, or per-query rotation. Every time a query lands on 8.8.8.8, the public internet truthfully answers NXDOMAIN for your private zone, and that negative answer can then be cached, which is why the failure sticks for a while.

Never mix internal and public resolvers in the same list. Fix: the VPN should push only 10.0.0.2, or better, use split DNS (systemd-resolved / dnsmasq) that routes *.corp.internal to 10.0.0.2 and everything else to the public resolver. Remove 8.8.8.8 from the VPN profile entirely.

Inbound email to us bounces from some senders with errors about the MX host. Our DNS:

example.com.  MX 10 mail.example.com.
mail.example.com.  CNAME host7.provider.net.
host7.provider.net.  A 198.51.100.23

Outbound mail works fine.

The MX target is a CNAME, and that is prohibited: RFC 2181 section 10.3 says an MX (or NS) record must point to a host name with A/AAAA records, never to an alias. Lenient MTAs follow the CNAME anyway, which is why only *some* senders bounce - strict MTAs reject the lookup or loop on it.

Fix: give mail.example.com its own address records and delete the CNAME:

mail.example.com.  A 198.51.100.23

(or point the MX directly at host7.provider.net if you do not need your own name). While you are there, confirm the PTR for 198.51.100.23 and your SPF record still line up with the name you choose, so you do not trade a routing bounce for a spam-folder problem.

We moved our site to a new IP 24 hours ago. The DNS record now shows the new IP with TTL 300, but roughly half our traffic still lands on the old server (its access log is busy). Is the change still propagating?

Nothing is broken, and "propagation" is the wrong model - nothing pushes the change out. What you are seeing is cache lifetime. Before the move, the record carried a long TTL (typically 86400, one day). Every resolver that fetched the old answer before your edit keeps serving it until *that cached copy* expires - up to a full day from when they fetched it, regardless of the TTL 300 on the new record. The 300 only governs fresh lookups.

Handle it this way:
- Keep the old server up and serving (or proxying to the new one) until its traffic decays to zero - plan the drain around the OLD TTL, not the new one.
- You can flush the big public caches (Google and Cloudflare both offer cache-purge pages) to speed up those resolvers.
- Next migration: lower the TTL to 300 at least one full old-TTL period *before* the move, so every cache in the world holds a short-lived copy when you flip the record.

We deleted the staging app last week, but staging.example.com still serves a page - our marketing homepage. DNS has no staging record; it does have:

*.example.com.  A 203.0.113.10

and the marketing site is the default virtual host on that IP.

The staging app is gone; the wildcard is impersonating it. A wildcard record matches any name that has no explicit record, so staging.example.com still resolves to 203.0.113.10. The web server at that IP finds no staging vhost and serves its default - the marketing site. Nothing is deployed; two defaults are stacking up to fake a live site.

Fix at either layer:
- DNS: add an explicit staging record that points where you intend (or to a parked address), overriding the wildcard - or delete the wildcard if it is not earning its keep.
- Server: make the default vhost return 404/410 instead of real content, so unknown names fail loudly.

Also audit what else the wildcard is quietly answering for - typos and other decommissioned names resolve too, which is why monitoring never complained: every name "works".

Browsers load our API fine, but curl from servers fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate". openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 shows a certificate chain of length 1 (just the leaf, CN=api.example.com) and ends with: Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate).

The server is sending an incomplete chain: only the leaf certificate. A client needs leaf -> intermediate -> root to build a trust path; with the intermediate missing, strict clients (curl, most server-side TLS stacks) stop at "unable to verify the first certificate" because the leaf's issuer is unknown to them.

Browsers mask this: they fetch missing intermediates via the AIA extension and cache intermediates from other sites, so the gap is invisible to your users but fatal to machine clients.

Fix on the server: serve the full chain - leaf + intermediate(s), in order. With certbot that is fullchain.pem, not cert.pem. Reload and re-test with the same openssl command: the chain should show depth 2 or more and Verify return code: 0.

certbot renew works for example.com but fails for api.example.com. The log says the CA could not fetch the challenge: GET http://api.example.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/x9f... returned 404. The token file definitely exists in the webroot, and the api vhost has a blanket rule: location / { return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } with the HTTPS vhost serving our SPA from a different root.

We hardened our servers by disabling TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Everything is fine except one partner integration, which now fails with "tlsv1 alert protocol version" in our logs. Their client turns out to be a very old Java application. Is our certificate broken?

Your certificate is fine - that alert is about protocol versions, not certificates. "tlsv1 alert protocol version" means the client offered only TLS versions your server now refuses (its old Java stack tops out at TLS 1.0/1.1), so the handshake died before any certificate was even evaluated. Every modern client works because they offer 1.2+.

Your options, in order:
1. Get the partner to upgrade or front their client with something modern - the only real fix.
2. If the integration is business-critical and cannot move yet, isolate the weakness: a separate hostname/listener for this partner alone, with legacy TLS enabled there, restricted by IP allowlist and mTLS if possible, and a documented removal date.
3. Do not re-enable TLS 1.0/1.1 on the main endpoint - that re-exposes every user to satisfy one legacy client.

Verify the main endpoint afterwards with openssl s_client -tls1_2 (connects) and -tls1_1 (refused).

https://shop.example.com presents a certificate for blog.example.com and serves the blog. Our nginx config has two server blocks: blog has "listen 443 ssl default_server;" and shop has only "listen 80;" plus a redirect. Both certs exist on disk. What is happening at the TLS layer?

A fleet of kiosks started reporting "certificate is not yet valid" for a certificate we issued yesterday. The servers and all our laptops are fine. On one kiosk: `date` shows a date six weeks in the past, and systemd-timesyncd logs say the time offset was too large to step safely; NTP became unreachable after a DHCP change last week.

The certificate is fine and the kiosks' clocks are the bug. Certificate validation compares the cert's validity window against the *client's* clock. The cert's notBefore is yesterday; a kiosk that believes it is six weeks ago sees a certificate "from the future" and rejects it. Your laptops agree with the server because their clocks are right.

The root cause chain is in your evidence: the DHCP change stopped handing the kiosks a reachable NTP source, their clocks drifted (and timesyncd declined to step a very large offset), and the problem only became *visible* when a freshly issued certificate made the skew matter.

Fix: restore NTP reachability for the kiosk network (DHCP option 42 and/or firewall UDP 123 to the time servers), force an initial sync (restart timesyncd or chronyc makestep), and then renew nothing - the existing cert will validate once the clocks are right. Add monitoring on clock offset (alert at, say, >30 seconds) so next time the page you get is "kiosk clocks drifting", weeks before certificates "break".

Our backup cron job starts (syslog shows it), but the dated output file comes out named just "backup-" with an empty suffix. The crontab line is:

0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup --name backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

The % characters are eating your command. In a crontab, % is special syntax, not a literal: the first % marks the end of the command, and everything after it is fed to the command as standard input. So cron actually runs:

backup --name backup-$(date +

and the rest of your format string (%Y%m%d) goes to stdin. The date command gets a bare "+" and prints an empty suffix - hence "backup-".

Fixes:
- Escape every percent in the crontab: backup-$(date +\%Y\%m\%d)
- Better: move the whole command into a script file and let cron call just the script. Inside a script, % is an ordinary character, and you also get a file you can run by hand to test.

This is the single most common reason a cron command behaves differently from the same text pasted into a shell.

My ETL script works perfectly when I run it, but the cron version fails. The cron mail says: /home/deploy/etl.sh: line 12: python: not found. Line 12 just calls `python` - the script uses a pyenv install that is on my PATH when I log in.

Cron does not run your shell - it runs the command with a minimal, fixed environment: a short PATH (typically /usr/bin:/bin), SHELL=/bin/sh, and none of your profile. Your interactive PATH includes pyenv's shims because your .bashrc adds them; cron never reads .bashrc. So `python` resolves for you and not for cron. This is the #1 cause of "works on my terminal, fails in cron".

Fixes:
- Set PATH explicitly at the top of the crontab (including the pyenv shims directory), or
- Call the interpreter by absolute path in the script (/home/deploy/.pyenv/shims/python), and set HOME in the crontab too if the script relies on ~ anywhere.

To reproduce cron's environment when debugging, run: env -i /bin/sh -c '/home/deploy/etl.sh' - if it fails there the same way, you have found a difference; fix until it passes.
I put a valid entry in /etc/cron.d/nightly-reports.sh on our Ubuntu servers. It never runs - no errors in syslog, nothing. The identical entry pasted into root's crontab works fine.

The filename is disqualifying it. Debian/Ubuntu's cron scans /etc/cron.d but silently ignores any file whose name contains characters outside letters, digits, underscore, and hyphen - the same naming rules as run-parts. The dot in "nightly-reports.sh" makes the file invisible to the scanner, and because it is skipped at scan time, there is no error to find in syslog. The entry itself can be perfect; it is never read.

Fix: rename the file to /etc/cron.d/nightly-reports (no extension), owned by root, mode 644 or 600, and make sure the file ends with a trailing newline (a missing final newline is the other silent killer in cron.d). Two format reminders for cron.d specifically, since it differs from a user crontab: the line needs the user field (e.g. `0 2 * * * root /usr/local/bin/reports`), and you do not need to restart cron - it re-reads the directory automatically.

Our hourly export job has grown slower - it now takes about 90 minutes. The output CSV sometimes contains interleaved, duplicated blocks of rows. During the window, ps shows two export processes running at once.

The scheduler does not prevent overlap, and your job now outlives its interval: the instance started at 10:00 is still running at 11:00 when the next one starts. Two processes appending to the same CSV interleave their writes - that is precisely the duplicated, interleaved blocks you are seeing. Nothing is wrong with the export logic itself.

Fix:
- Serialize it: flock -n /var/lock/export.lock /usr/local/bin/export in the cron line makes a second instance exit immediately instead of piling in. (Or move the schedule to a systemd timer + service - systemd will not start a second copy of a unit that is already running.)
- Make the output atomic regardless: write to a temp file and rename it over the target when done, so readers never see a half-written file even if something else goes wrong.
- Then treat the 90-minute runtime as its own problem - a job that keeps growing will eventually overlap by two.

A cron job of ours has been failing for weeks and nobody noticed. Syslog shows the job DOES start every night (CMD lines are there), and when we run the script by hand it prints a clear error. The crontab has MAILTO="" at the top, and this minimal server has no mail service configured.

The job's errors had nowhere to go, by configuration. Cron's only built-in reporting channel is mail: anything a job writes to stdout/stderr is mailed to the crontab's owner (or MAILTO). You set MAILTO="" - which explicitly disables that mail - on a box with no MTA anyway. So every night the script printed its error into a channel that was switched off, and cron's syslog lines only record that the command *started*, not what it said or how it exited. "It runs" and "it works" were never the same fact.

Fix:
- Give job output a durable home: append an explicit redirect in the cron line, e.g. `... /usr/local/bin/job >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1`, and alert on non-zero exits (or have the script log to the journal with logger).
- Remove the MAILTO="" unless silence is truly intended - and if it is, replace mail with an actual monitoring check on the job's success marker.

Standing rule: for every scheduled job, be able to answer "where does its output go, and who sees a failure?" before you need it.

df says /var is 100% full (80G used), but du -x /var totals only about 31G. lsof +L1 shows this line:

java  4123  app  87w  REG  253,1  48000000000  0 9912 /var/log/app/app.log.1 (deleted)

Where is the space?

The space is in that deleted file. lsof +L1 lists files that have been unlinked but are still open - and your JVM is holding a 48GB rotated log in exactly that state. When a file is deleted while a process has it open, the directory entry disappears (so du, which walks paths, cannot see it) but the data blocks are not freed until the last descriptor closes (so df, which counts blocks, still charges you for them). du and df are both telling the truth about different things; the ~49G gap between them is this file.

To reclaim it:
- Cleanest: restart or reload the process so it closes the descriptor - the blocks free immediately.
- Without a restart: truncate through the proc filesystem, `: > /proc/4123/fd/87`, which releases the blocks while the process keeps running.
- Then fix the cause: your rotation is renaming/deleting a file the app never reopens - switch to copytruncate or add a postrotate reopen signal, or this refills.

Applications are failing with "No space left on device" when creating files, but df -h shows the filesystem only 58% used. df -i shows IUse% at 100%. A find count says /var/lib/php/sessions contains about 4.2 million files. Our php.ini has session.gc_probability = 0.

You are out of inodes, not bytes. Every file needs an inode; df -h says 42% of your *space* is free while df -i says 0% of your *inodes* are. Millions of tiny files - here, PHP session files - exhaust inodes long before they dent capacity, and session files accumulate without limit because you disabled the garbage collector that deletes them: with gc_probability = 0 and no external cleanup job, every session ever created is still on disk.

Fix:
- Delete stale session files now (find /var/lib/php/sessions -type f -mmin +1440 -delete, adjusting the age to your session lifetime) and watch df -i recover.
- Restore cleanup permanently: re-enable session GC (gc_probability > 0) or the distro's session-cleaner timer - and check why it was disabled; on Debian/Ubuntu the cleaner is a cron/timer that expects gc_probability=0, so make sure exactly one mechanism owns it.
- Longer term, sessions in Redis or a database remove the inode pressure entirely. Alert on inode usage, not just disk usage - this failure is invisible to a bytes-only monitor.

Our MySQL primary went effectively read-only at 03:00. The error log repeats: "Disk is full writing './binlog.000812' (OS errno 28). Waiting for someone to free space..." The binlog directory holds 190G of binlogs. The replica stopped two days ago with an authentication error, and our binlog purge was tied to the backup job, which has also been failing.

The chain is: replica broke -> backups started failing -> binlog purging (which was coupled to the backup job) stopped -> binlogs grew unbounded for two days -> disk filled -> MySQL could not write the next binlog entry, and since every write transaction needs a binlog entry, the server blocked writes. It looks read-only, but it is really write-blocked on disk.

Recover in this order:
1. Free space *outside* the binlogs first (old OS logs, temp files, anything expendable). Never rm binlog files directly - that corrupts the binlog index and can make recovery far worse.
2. Once MySQL can breathe, purge properly through SQL: PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'binlog.000800' (or by date), which updates the index safely.
3. Fix the replica's authentication error and the backup job - they are the actual root causes.
4. Decouple retention from backups: set binlog_expire_logs_seconds so binlogs expire on age regardless, and alert on replica status and disk *trend* - two days of warnings preceded this.

/var/log grew by 60G in one day after a deploy. The biggest file is app-debug.log at 58G. The deploy diff flipped LOG_LEVEL from INFO to DEBUG in the app config. Our logrotate entry for the app logs is "weekly, rotate 4". A teammate insists rotation is broken.

Rotation is not broken - it is weekly, and the firehose is the deploy. At DEBUG level this app is writing ~2.5G per hour (per-request SQL and payload logging adds up fast), so a day of DEBUG produces 58G long before the weekly rotation gets a chance to run. logrotate's schedule never had a vote.

Fix:
- Set LOG_LEVEL back to INFO and restart/reload - that stops the growth at the source.
- Reclaim now: force a rotation (logrotate -f) or truncate the debug file after confirming nothing needs it.
- Guardrails: add a size trigger to the rotation policy (maxsize) for this log so volume spikes rotate early, and alert on log *growth rate* - 60G/day is detectable within the hour.
- One more reason to revert quickly: DEBUG logs in production often contain request payloads - check what sensitive data just got written to disk for a day, and treat retention of that file accordingly.

Since the November fall-back, our daily sales report's "yesterday" totals are wrong - the window looks shifted by an hour, sometimes including an hour of the wrong day. The pipeline converts event timestamps to local time using a fixed offset of -05:00 before bucketing them by date.

The fixed offset is the bug, and the fall-back is what exposed it. Your zone is not -05:00 all year: it is -04:00 (EDT) until the first Sunday of November and -05:00 (EST) after. A converter hard-coded to -05:00 was wrong by an hour all summer in the other direction (or the pipeline was built during winter and never correct in summer); the moment the real offset changed, the bucket boundaries moved an hour and started slicing days at 01:00 local instead of midnight - hence totals that include an hour of the neighboring day.

Fix: convert with the named time zone (America/New_York), whose rules know which offset applies on which date - in Python, zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("America/New_York"); in SQL, AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'. Store timestamps in UTC and apply the zone only at bucketing/reporting time. Then re-run the affected days' reports: every day since the transition (and, honestly, every day the fixed offset was in force) has mis-bucketed edges.

Our reminder job is configured for 09:00 America/New_York. It fired at 09:00 all winter, but since the March spring-forward it fires at 10:00. The scheduler's stored config says: tz_offset: -05:00 (captured when we set it up in January).

The scheduler never stored the time zone - it stored the offset in effect on the day you configured it. "09:00 at a fixed -05:00" means 14:00 UTC, every day, forever. While EST is in effect that is 09:00 local and everything looks right. The day EDT begins, 14:00 UTC becomes 10:00 local - so the job now fires an hour late, and it will keep doing so until November, when it silently becomes correct again. (Jobs created in summer have the mirror-image bug: set up at -04:00, they fire an hour early all winter.)

Fix: configure the job with the IANA zone name, America/New_York, so the offset is looked up from the DST rules for each run date instead of frozen at setup. Audit every job created the same way - any config holding a numeric offset instead of a zone name carries this bug for half the year.
Our billing job runs at 01:30 local time. On Nov 1 it ran TWICE - the log shows executions at 05:30 UTC and 06:30 UTC, both stamped 01:30 local. Did the scheduler glitch?

No glitch - Nov 1 is the fall-back transition, and 01:30 happens twice that night. At 05:30 UTC the local time was 01:30 EDT; clocks then fell back, and at 06:30 UTC local time was 01:30 EST. A scheduler defined in local time correctly fires in both instances of the repeated hour, because both are legitimately "01:30".

How to prevent a repeat:
- Schedule jobs that must run exactly once in UTC, or move them outside the 01:00-02:00 window.
- Make the job idempotent regardless: at start, insert a run row keyed by the business date (unique constraint) and exit if it already exists. Only the winner proceeds.

Also check what the second run actually did - if it re-sent invoices or re-charged, dedupe on that same business-date key when you clean up.

Our signup dashboard and our database report disagree by a few dozen signups every day. The dashboard groups by the browser's local date (our team is in Tokyo, UTC+9); the API returns UTC timestamps. The mismatches all involve signups between midnight and 09:00 Tokyo time.

Both numbers are "correct" - they are counting different windows. Midnight in Tokyo is 15:00 UTC the previous day, so every signup from 00:00-09:00 JST belongs to the previous UTC date. The database report buckets by UTC date; the dashboard buckets by JST date; the few dozen in the gap are exactly the signups in that 9-hour offset window, which is why the discrepancy tracks overnight traffic volume.

Fix: pick ONE reporting time zone for the business (usually the business's home zone) and bucket there consistently. Best is server-side: have the API aggregate with an explicit zone - e.g. (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo')::date - and return finished dates, so no client can silently redefine the day with its own locale.

After scaling our app from 4 to 12 instances, PostgreSQL started rejecting connections: "sorry, too many clients already" and sometimes "remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections". Each app instance has pool max 25. PostgreSQL max_connections is 200.

It is arithmetic, not a database fault. Twelve instances x 25 pool connections = 300 potential connections against a server limit of 200. At 4 instances you peaked at 100 and never noticed. The "reserved slots" variant appears because the last few slots are held for superusers, so ordinary app connections are refused first.

Fixes, in order of preference:
- Put PgBouncer (transaction pooling) between the app and PostgreSQL: app pools stay as they are, but the server sees one small capped pool (say 40) multiplexed across all instances.
- Or shrink each instance's pool: 12 x 12 = 144 leaves headroom under 200 - and count background workers, migrations, and admin sessions in the budget, because max_connections covers them too.

Raising max_connections alone is the weakest option: every PostgreSQL connection is a process with real memory cost.

Our connection pool's active count climbs steadily from 5 to the max of 50 over about 6 hours and never comes back down; then threads start timing out waiting for connections. Restarting the app resets it. The only suspicious log entry is a NullPointerException that sometimes appears in the nightly report export.

A monotonic climb that only a restart cures is the signature of a leak, not of load - load goes up *and down*. The exception is your prime suspect: the classic pattern is borrow a connection, use it, close it on the happy path - and when the export throws (your NPE), the close is skipped and the connection is never returned. A few leaks a day times a 50-connection pool gives you exactly this six-hour sawtooth.

Fix:
- Close every borrowed connection with try-with-resources (or finally), on every code path, starting with the export.
- Turn on the pool's leak detection (e.g. Hikari leakDetectionThreshold ~30s) temporarily: it logs the borrow stack trace of connections held too long, which names the leaking call sites directly instead of you auditing everything.
- Verify after the fix that the active count returns to baseline when load stops - that is the leak test.

We keep getting "connection is not available" pool errors, so I assumed a leak. But pg_stat_activity shows about 40 sessions in state=active, all running the same orders report query, each already running 20-40 seconds. Pool size is 50.

Your own evidence rules the leak out: leaked connections sit *idle*, holding slots while doing nothing. Yours are all actively running one query class. This is throughput collapse, not leakage: a query that takes 20-40 seconds occupies a slot the whole time, so 40 concurrent arrivals of it consume nearly the entire pool and everyone else queues until timeout.

Fix the query, not the pool:
- Run EXPLAIN on it - a report query like this is almost always doing a sequential scan for want of an index on the join/filter column. Add the index and watch the runtime fall to milliseconds.
- Set a statement_timeout so a runaway query cannot hold a slot indefinitely.
- Resist raising the pool size: it would only let *more* 40-second scans run concurrently and make the database slower.

Database CPU pegs at 100% for about two minutes at the top of every hour. App logs show thousands of simultaneous "cache miss" entries for the key home:feed. That key's TTL is 3600 seconds and regenerating it takes a ~3 second query.

A textbook cache stampede, with the clockwork regularity as the tell. One very hot key, a TTL that expires on a predictable boundary, and thousands of requests arriving in the same seconds - every one of them sees a miss and launches the same 3-second regeneration query simultaneously. The database is not slow; it is being asked to do the same expensive work thousands of times in parallel.

Fixes:
- Single-flight regeneration: guard the rebuild with a per-key lock (or a library's request coalescing) so one request rebuilds while the rest serve the stale value or wait briefly.
- Stale-while-revalidate: serve the expired value during regeneration instead of treating expiry as a cliff.
- Jitter TTLs (3600 +/- a few hundred seconds, randomized per write) so keys stop expiring in lockstep.

Short-term bandage: pre-warm home:feed from a cron a minute before the hour.

After every deploy, database load spikes and latency doubles for about 15 minutes, then recovers. Our cache hit ratio drops to nearly 0 at exactly deploy times. Cache keys look like "v2.4.1:user:123" - the prefix is the app release version.

You are invalidating your entire cache on every deploy, on purpose, without noticing. Because the release version is part of every key, the new version of the app looks up v2.4.2:user:123 while the cache is full of v2.4.1:user:123 - every key misses at once, every request falls through to the database, and the "deploy problem" is really a self-inflicted cold cache that takes 15 minutes to re-warm.

Fix: version cache keys by *data schema*, not by release. Only bump the prefix when the stored value's format actually changes (which is rare and deliberate), and keep a deploy-time cache warmer for the hottest keys if cold starts still hurt. A side benefit: during a rollback, the old version's keys are still warm, so rolling back stops being a second outage.

Our Redis cache hit ratio has degraded over the last week. INFO shows: used_memory at the 4G maxmemory, policy allkeys-lru, evicted_keys climbing steadily. A nightly analytics job writes a handful of keys like report:2026-11-25:full that are ~200MB each.

The analytics job is evicting your cache. Under allkeys-lru, every key competes in one pool: when the nightly job inserts several 200MB report blobs into a 4G instance that is already at maxmemory, Redis must evict roughly that much *other* data - which in practice means thousands of the small, hot keys your application actually depends on. Hit ratio then degrades until the working set re-warms, and next night it happens again.

Fix:
- Separate the workloads: batch artifacts belong in their own Redis instance (or object storage - a 200MB report is not cache data at all). Never let bulk writers share an eviction pool with a latency cache.
- Cap value sizes at the client as a guardrail, and alert on the evicted_keys *rate* - evictions beginning at all is the signal, not something to discover from hit ratio a week later.
- For the application cache, allkeys-lfu usually protects the genuinely hot set better than lru if this pattern recurs.

During a 10-minute partial outage of an upstream service, that upstream received about 27x its normal request volume from us. Our configs: the mobile API client retries 3 times, the API gateway retries 3 times, and the service's own HTTP client retries 3 times - all with immediate retries, no delays configured anywhere.

Your retries multiplied. Each layer's retries are independent, so one user action can become 3 (client) x 3 (gateway) x 3 (service client) = 27 upstream attempts - and your logs confirm exactly that factor. Because every retry is immediate, the amplification lands in the same seconds the upstream is least able to cope: retries turned a partial outage into a self-inflicted denial of service, and probably extended it.

Fix the architecture, not the numbers:
- Retry in ONE layer only - the one closest to the operation that understands idempotency - and disable retries in the others.
- Exponential backoff with full jitter (e.g. base 200ms, doubling, randomized), so retries spread out instead of arriving as a synchronized volley.
- A retry budget and a circuit breaker: if retries exceed ~10% of requests, or the upstream is failing fast, stop retrying and fail quickly until it recovers.
- Only auto-retry idempotent operations; a retried non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key to be safe.

Timeline from last night: 02:10 one of our 6 app nodes slows down (long GC pauses). The load balancer health check (every 2s, eject after 2 failures) removes it. 02:14 two more nodes fail their checks and are ejected. 02:19 the site is effectively down, even though the remaining nodes' processes never crashed.

This is a health-check cascade: the checker killed the site, not the nodes. Removing one of six nodes pushed ~20% more load onto each survivor, raising their latency and GC pressure. Their health checks - an aggressive 2-second interval with only 2 failures to eject, and presumably a timeout the now-slower nodes could not meet - started failing, so more nodes were ejected, concentrating load further. Each ejection made the next one more likely: a positive feedback loop that ends at zero capacity with every process still running.

Fixes:
- Make checks less trigger-happy: longer timeout, more consecutive failures before ejection, and check a cheap dedicated health endpoint rather than a real request path.
- Cap ejection: never remove more than a fixed fraction (e.g. 50%) of the pool via health checks - if "everyone is failing", the checker or the load is the problem, and keeping some capacity beats none.
- Shed load deliberately (queue, return 503 for low-priority traffic) instead of letting latency decide for you.
- And fix the original GC issue - it was the trigger, just not the cause of the outage.

One consumer is stuck: the log shows message id msg-88412 being processed over and over - about 40,000 attempts in an hour, each ending in a JSON parse exception. The queue is FIFO and has no dead-letter configuration. Everything behind that message is starving.

msg-88412 is a poison message. It deterministically crashes the consumer (a payload the parser cannot handle - typically a field a schema change removed), the consumer nacks it, and the broker immediately redelivers it because there is no attempt limit or dead-letter queue configured. On a FIFO queue it is worse: the poison message sits at the head, so it is not just looping, it is blocking every message behind it.

Fix in order:
1. Stop the bleeding: configure a maximum delivery count (3-5 attempts) with a dead-letter queue as the destination, and let msg-88412 land there so the queue drains.
2. Diagnose from the DLQ copy: compare the payload against what the parser expects - the schema drift will be visible.
3. Fix the parser to handle (or explicitly reject to the DLQ) that shape, then replay the DLQ.
4. Alert on redeliveries per message id; 40,000 attempts should have paged someone at attempt 10.

We deployed a bad release, rolled the code back within 10 minutes - and the errors continued. The rolled-back code logs: column "users.legacy_status" does not exist. The bad release's migration had dropped that column and renamed another one.

A code rollback is not a system rollback. Your migration moved the schema forward irreversibly, and the old binary depends on exactly what the migration deleted. The rollback restored the code to a state that is incompatible with the database it now runs against - which is why the outage survived the rollback.

Recover first, philosophize second:
- Fastest safe path is usually forward: re-add legacy_status as a nullable column (restoring its data if the migration or a backup preserved it) so the old code runs, or redeploy the new code if its fault was smaller than this one. Do not improvise a down-migration against production under pressure unless the migration shipped one.
- Process fix, so this class dies: expand/contract migrations. Release N adds the new column and dual-writes; reads switch over; the old column is dropped in release N+1 or later - never in the same release that stops using it. At every point in that sequence, the previous code version still works against the current schema, which is precisely the property a rollback needs.

After a rollback, users report blank pages. Browser logs show index.html loads, but app.8f3c.js returns 404 - that hash belongs to the release we rolled back FROM. Our CDN caches index.html at the edge for 1 hour, and during the incident someone purged the JS files from the CDN cache.

This is version skew between HTML and assets, created by the incident response. The edge is still serving the *new* release's index.html from its 1-hour cache. That HTML references the new release's hashed bundle, app.8f3c.js. But the origin has been rolled back (so it no longer serves that file) and the purge deleted the edge's cached copy - so the asset 404s and the page renders blank. The rollback itself was fine; the purge broke it.

Fix now: republish the missing hashed assets to the origin (they are immutable files; keep every release's assets deployed - they cost almost nothing) and purge or wait out the stale index.html.
Fix permanently:
- index.html should be no-cache or very short TTL at the edge; hashed assets get the long TTL. HTML is the pointer - if the pointer can be stale for an hour, skew is guaranteed eventually.
- Never purge prior releases' assets during an incident. Old assets existing is what makes rollbacks safe.

We rolled back our worker deployment, but jobs stopped being processed - the workers are up and idle. During the incident, someone changed the queue name in our platform's dashboard from jobs-main to jobs-main-v2. The repo config says jobs-main, the workers' startup logs say "listening on jobs-main", and the producers are publishing to jobs-main-v2.

Your own logs contain the whole diagnosis: producers publish to jobs-main-v2, workers listen on jobs-main. The system is healthy on both sides of an empty gap. The rollback only restored what is in git - the dashboard change was made out-of-band during the incident, was never committed, and therefore survived the rollback and now disagrees with the code's configuration. Configuration drift, not a code bug.

Fix now: align the two sides (point the workers at jobs-main-v2 or the producers back to jobs-main - pick the side with the jobs you care about; the queued jobs are sitting in v2).
Fix the class: configuration lives in exactly one place, version-controlled and deployed by the same pipeline as code, so a rollback restores code and config together. Dashboard edits during incidents are sometimes necessary - the rule is they get committed to the repo as part of the incident cleanup, and the workers' startup log line printing the *effective* queue (which is how you caught this) is worth having on every service.

I updated DATABASE_URL in /etc/app/app.env and restarted the service, but it still connects to the old database. The systemd unit contains both of these:

Environment=DATABASE_URL=postgres://old-db:5432/app
EnvironmentFile=/etc/app/app.env

`systemctl cat app` confirms both lines are there.

The unit file is overriding your env file. In systemd, when a variable is set both by an EnvironmentFile and by an Environment= assignment in the unit, the explicit Environment= in the unit wins (unit settings take precedence over the file, and among multiple Environment= lines the last one stands). Your edit to app.env is being read - and then immediately shadowed by the stale hard-coded line in the unit. That is why the restart changed nothing.

Fix: delete the Environment=DATABASE_URL line from the unit so configuration lives in exactly one place (the env file), then systemctl daemon-reload and restart. Verify with `systemctl show app -p Environment` and the app's startup log showing the new host. Also check for drop-ins (systemctl cat shows them too) - a stale override in /etc/systemd/system/app.service.d/ would shadow both.

I changed API_BASE under build.args in docker-compose.yml and ran docker compose up -d, but docker exec app printenv API_BASE still shows the old value. The Dockerfile has:

ARG API_BASE=https://api.example.com
ENV API_BASE=$API_BASE

docker inspect shows the image was built three weeks ago.

Nothing rebuilt your image, so nothing changed. ARG exists only at build time: its value is baked into the image through the ENV line when the image is built. `docker compose up -d` recreates containers from the *existing* image - and your inspect output shows that image is three weeks old, so it still carries the old API_BASE in its environment. Compose correctly decided nothing it manages had changed.

Fix for today: docker compose up -d --build.
Fix for the design: runtime configuration does not belong in the image. Pass API_BASE through `environment:` in compose (or an env file) instead - environment: entries override the image's baked ENV at container start, take effect on a plain recreate, and let one image serve every environment. Reserve ARG for things that genuinely vary at build time.

Our new cache servers are being ignored. At boot the app logs: "cache: connecting to 127.0.0.1:6379". The deploy manifest sets REDIS_URI=redis://cache-1.internal:6379. The app's config code reads an environment variable named REDIS_URL and defaults to redis://127.0.0.1:6379 when it is unset.

A one-word typo with a silent fallback is the whole bug. The manifest provides REDIS_URI; the app reads REDIS_URL. The variable it wants is never set, so it uses its built-in default - localhost - and because a default exists, nothing fails loudly: in development a local Redis makes it look correct, and in production it quietly talks to nothing (or to an accidental local instance). The boot log line is the giveaway: the app is telling you the *effective* endpoint, and it is not the one you deployed.

Fix:
- Correct the name in the manifest (REDIS_URL), redeploy, and confirm the boot log now shows cache-1.internal.
- Remove the failure mode: required configuration should fail fast at startup when unset in production - a crash loop on a missing REDIS_URL would have paged you in a minute instead of silently degrading.
- Keep that startup logging of effective endpoints (with secrets redacted) - it is what made this diagnosable from one log line.

Deploys keep failing at startup: the new instance exits with "bind: address already in use :8080". ss -ltnp shows port 8080 held by a process started yesterday whose PPID is 1. Our app spawns a helper subprocess at startup. The systemd unit sets KillMode=process.

Your old instance never fully died. KillMode=process tells systemd to kill only the main process on stop/restart. The helper subprocess survives, gets reparented to PID 1 (exactly what your ss output shows), and - because it inherited the listening socket from its parent - it keeps port 8080 bound. The new instance then cannot bind and exits. Every deploy leaves the port one generation behind.

Fix now: kill the stale PID holding 8080, then start the service.
Fix permanently: remove KillMode=process (the default, control-group, kills every process in the unit's cgroup together) - KillMode=process is almost never what you want for a service that spawns children. Belt and braces: have the helper not inherit the listener (close-on-exec on the socket, or have the helper open its own sockets after start), and after each deploy verify with ss that exactly one process owns 8080.

After reboots, SOMETIMES our metrics exporter fails with "listen tcp :9090: bind: address already in use" - and other times the app itself fails with the same error and the exporter starts fine. Both configs specify port 9090: the app's built-in metrics server and the standalone exporter.

Two services are racing for one port, and boot order is the coin flip. Both the app's metrics server and the exporter are configured to bind 9090. Whichever starts first wins; the loser logs "address already in use" and dies. Because service startup order varies between boots (parallel unit startup, timing), the *victim* varies too - which is why the failure looks random and why restarting the loser "fixes" it until the next reboot reshuffles the race.

Fix: assign distinct ports in configuration management - exporter keeps the conventional 9090, the app's metrics move to 9091 (or the app drops its built-in metrics endpoint if the exporter replaces it). Then prevent recurrence: add a deploy-time check that fails when two units on the same host claim the same listen port - port inventories are cheap, boot-order heisenbugs are not.

nginx will not start on a fresh VM: "bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use)". Our nginx config is the same one we use everywhere. ss -ltnp shows:

LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("apache2",pid=812,fd=4))

Your config is fine - port 80 is already owned by Apache, which came pre-installed and enabled in the base image even though nobody chose it. bind() fails before nginx reads a single directive, which is why the identical config works on your other VMs.

Fix: `systemctl disable --now apache2` (or remove the package), then start nginx and confirm with ss that nginx owns 80/443. The general lesson: when a bind fails on a "fresh" box, inventory the listeners first - base images routinely ship enabled services nobody asked for.

Since we enabled log rotation, /var/log/app/app.log is always nearly empty, yet the disk keeps growing. lsof shows:

app  2210 app  3w  REG  253,1  48234496000  9912 /var/log/app/app.log.1 (deleted)

Our logrotate block renames the file and creates a new one; there is no postrotate script, and the app has no log-reopen logic.

The app is still writing to the old file. Rotation renamed app.log to app.log.1 and created a fresh app.log, but the process holds an open descriptor to the *inode*, not the name - so its writes keep going to the renamed file, and your new app.log stays empty. When the next rotation deleted app.log.1, the file became nameless but the writes (and the 48 GB) persist until the process exits - that is the invisible disk growth, and your logs for the whole period are effectively in a deleted file.

Fix, either:
- Add a postrotate that signals the app to reopen its log (SIGHUP/SIGUSR1, whatever it supports): `postrotate /bin/kill -HUP $(cat /run/app.pid) endscript`, or
- Use `copytruncate` if the app cannot reopen (accepting the small copy race).

Verify after the next rotation with lsof: the descriptor should point at the live app.log.

logrotate silently stopped rotating /var/log/app. Running it with debug output shows:

error skipping "/var/log/app/app.log" because parent directory has insecure permissions (It's world writable or writable by group which is not "root"). Set "su" directive in config to avoid this error.

A deploy script chmod'ed /var/log/app to 777 last month to "fix a permission problem".

logrotate is refusing on purpose, and it told you why: rotating root-owned logs inside a world-writable directory is a symlink-attack risk, so it skips the file rather than follow unsafe paths. The chmod 777 is the root cause; the rotation failure is the symptom.

Fix properly:
1. Restore sane ownership/permissions: the directory should be owned by root or the app user with mode 0755 - not world-writable. (Fix the original permission problem by giving the app write access as the owner or via group, not 777.)
2. Add an `su` directive to that log's block naming the user/group that owns the directory, e.g. `su app adm`, so logrotate knows which identity rotation is safe under.

Then force one run (`logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/app`) and confirm the state file advances and a rotated file appears.

We are investigating an incident from 02:00 last night, but the app logs jump from 01:59 straight to 05:12. Rotation config is daily with maxsize 100M, rotate 4, and logrotate runs hourly. Overnight, a verbose upstream bug produced about 30x normal log volume. The four rotated files on disk are all timestamped between 02:00 and 05:00.

Your retention ate the incident. Retention was counted in *files* (rotate 4), not in time - and with maxsize triggering hourly runs at 30x volume, those four files covered only about three hours. Each rotation pushed the oldest file off the end, so by 05:12 the 02:00 window had been rotated out of existence. The timestamps on the surviving files prove the mechanism.

Fixes:
- Size retention for worst-case volume, not average: if four files must cover a week at 30x volume, you need far more of them (or time-based retention with enough disk).
- The real fix for forensics: ship logs off the box in near-real-time (agent to central storage), so local rotation can never destroy the only copy.
- Alert on rotation frequency itself - rotating hourly instead of daily was an early, visible symptom of the same verbose bug.

In Kubernetes, lookups for the short name "db" from some pods return a public IP, 203.0.113.44, instead of failing. A pod's resolv.conf:

search billing.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local corp.example.com
options ndots:5

There is no Service named db (it is db-main). Our public zone corp.example.com has a wildcard A record pointing at our website.

This is the ndots + search-domain + wildcard trap, and every element is in your evidence. "db" has zero dots, and ndots:5 means the resolver tries it against *every* search domain before treating it as absolute. billing.svc..., svc..., cluster.local all miss - but corp.example.com is a real public domain with a wildcard, so the query db.corp.example.com *succeeds*, returning your website's public IP. Instead of an error, the app silently connects to the wrong place.

Fix:
- Use fully qualified names in app config: db-main.billing.svc.cluster.local - no search expansion involved.
- Remove corp.example.com from the pod search list (it leaks in from the node's resolv.conf via the default dnsPolicy); cluster search domains are the only ones pods should have.
- Treat "wildcard record + that domain in a search path" as a standing footgun anywhere, not just in Kubernetes.

Old Android 7/8 clients report "certificate expired" for our site, but the leaf certificate expires next year and desktop browsers are fine. The chain we serve is: leaf -> R3 intermediate -> "DST Root CA X3" (expired 2021-09-30). openssl verify with an old trust store fails at that last element.

The leaf is fine; one *path* through your served chain is not. The chain includes a cross-signed root that expired in 2021 - it was kept in the chain for compatibility with old Android, which does not check the expiry of a trust anchor the same way. Modern clients build the alternate path (leaf -> R3 -> ISRG Root X1) and never notice. The old clients you are hearing from are selecting the path that ends at the expired cross-sign and reporting the chain as expired - correctly, for that path.

Fix: serve the shorter chain - leaf + R3 only, dropping the expired cross-signed element. openssl verify with the old bundle should then reach the self-signed ISRG root in the store. Be explicit about the tradeoff you are making: devices old enough to *need* the cross-sign (pre-2016 Android without the ISRG root) lose access - that is a product decision, but keeping an expired element in the chain is not a stable way to serve them either.

Our nightly report script runs under cron and produces an EMPTY report, but works when I run it by hand. It opens data/orders.csv by relative path and never errors. There is an old, empty orders.csv sitting in the home directory from a test months ago.

The script is reading the wrong file, silently. Cron starts every job with its working directory set to the user's home directory; you run the script from the project directory. The relative path data/orders.csv resolves to ~/data/orders.csv under cron - and because that stale test file exists, the open succeeds and the script happily processes an empty file instead of crashing. No error is exactly what you would expect from this bug.

Fix:
- Anchor paths to the script's location: cd "$(dirname "$0")" at the top, or build absolute paths - never depend on the caller's working directory.
- Make the job fail loudly on nonsense input: an orders file that is empty or older than a day should exit non-zero and alert, not produce an empty report. Silent success on bad input is what turned a trivial path bug into a data incident.

Host disk / is at 97%, but du of the usual directories does not find the space. `docker system df` shows container writable layers are the biggest consumer, and one container's layer is 45G. The app inside writes temp export files to its own /tmp; our cleanup job cleans the host's /tmp and reports success. Where are the files, physically?

Inside the container's writable layer - an overlay2 upperdir on the host (under /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff), which is why a du of application paths never sees them: on the host they do not live at any path the app team thinks to measure, and the cleanup job has been diligently emptying the wrong /tmp (the host's) while the container's /tmp grew for months.

Fix:
- Reclaim now: remove the stale exports from inside the container (docker exec ... rm, or recreate the container if the layer is disposable) and watch df recover.
- Fix the cause: the app must clean its own temp files (trap/finally, or a sidecar cron *inside* the container's world), or write exports to a mounted volume with a retention policy the host can actually enforce.
- Check the other usual suspect while you are there: per-container JSON logs (docker ps --size shows both) - and alert on per-container disk, not just host disk, so the layer is visible before 97%.

We failed our database over to a new primary; DNS for db.internal now returns the new IP, and every system reconnected - except our Java service, which kept connecting to the old IP for hours until we restarted it. `getent hosts db.internal` on the same box returns the new IP. The JVM was started with default settings.

The JVM is caching DNS answers that the OS has long forgotten. Java's built-in DNS cache keeps successful lookups for a policy-controlled TTL - and in many distributions and hardened images that policy is effectively "cache forever" (networkaddress.cache.ttl = -1, historically the default when a security manager is present, and some base images set it explicitly). getent bypasses the JVM cache, which is why the box looks correct while the process disagrees. Restarting "fixed" it because a fresh JVM re-resolves.

Two layers to fix:
- Set a sane TTL: networkaddress.cache.ttl=30 in java.security, or -Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=30 at launch, so the JVM follows DNS changes within a minute.
- Make the connection pool survive failovers without a restart: validate connections on borrow and replace dead ones, so pooled connections to the old primary are discarded instead of reused.

Any long-lived runtime with its own resolver cache (not just Java) has this failure mode - it belongs on your failover runbook checklist.

Our payment provider shows TWO successful charges for order #5519, same amount, 40 seconds apart. Our logs show the first attempt timed out at the gateway's 30-second limit and our client retried the POST. No idempotency key was sent. The provider insists both charges are legitimate requests.

Both charges *are* legitimate requests - that is the problem. A timeout does not mean the first attempt failed; it means its outcome is unknown. The provider processed the first charge successfully but the response arrived after your 30-second cutoff, so your client, seeing a timeout, retried - and with no idempotency key, the provider had no way to know the second POST was the same purchase. It charged again. The provider is right; the bug is in the retry policy.

Fix:
- Refund the duplicate charge for #5519 now.
- Send an Idempotency-Key with every payment POST (derived from the order, stable across retries of the same purchase). The provider can then dedupe retries instead of double-charging.
- On timeout, reconcile before retrying: query the provider for the original attempt's status by order/key. Only retry when you know the first attempt did not succeed.
- Standing rule: a non-idempotent POST is never retried blind.

The guard is doing exactly what it is designed to do, and it is the bug. Non-interactive shells (like the one sshd creates for ssh host 'deploy.sh') still source ~/.bashrc - but they hit the `*) return` branch and exit the file *before* reaching the nvm lines, so PATH never gets set. Interactive logins pass the *i* check and continue to the nvm setup. Same file, same script, two different environments.

Fixes, any one of them:
- Move the PATH/tool setup *above* the guard (keep the guard for the interactive-only stuff below it - prompts, aliases).
- Or have the deploy script set up its own environment: source nvm explicitly or call node by absolute path. Scripts that depend on the caller's shell state are fragile regardless.
- Or load nvm from ~/.profile for login shells.

Do not just delete the guard - it exists to keep non-interactive shells from choking on interactive configuration.

The app tier says PostgreSQL is down after a config change, but psql on the database host works fine. ss -ltn on the DB host shows only:

127.0.0.1:5432

The change ticket says listen_addresses was set from '*' to 'localhost' during a security pass.

PostgreSQL is not down - it is deaf. listen_addresses='localhost' makes it bind only to the loopback interface, so the ss output shows it listening on 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. Every check run *on the box* succeeds; every connection from the app tier hits a host that is not listening on its network interface and fails. The security change confused "restrict who may connect" with "stop listening".

Fix: set listen_addresses back to '*' (or the specific interface IPs you want), then restart PostgreSQL - this setting is not reloadable. Keep the security goal, but enforce it at the right layer: pg_hba.conf lines scoped to the app subnet (and the firewall), which control *who* may authenticate without changing *where* the server listens. Verify with ss that 0.0.0.0:5432 (or the interface IP) is back, and test a connection from an app host, not from the DB host.

During a 2-hour incident our Python service appeared to log nothing at all - then, when the process exited, about 40,000 log lines appeared at once. The timestamps inside those lines span the whole 2 hours. The service writes to stdout, which is piped to a file.

The events were logged; they were just never flushed. When Python's stdout is a terminal it is line-buffered, but when it is a pipe or a file it switches to block buffering - output accumulates in a buffer (and in your logging handlers' buffers) and only reaches the file when the buffer fills or the process exits cleanly. During the hang, the buffer held two hours of evidence hostage; the exit flushed it all at once, which is why the timestamps are spread correctly but the arrival was a single burst. You were flying blind precisely when you needed the logs most.

Fix:
- Run with PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 (or python -u) for services, so stdout is unbuffered regardless of destination.
- Set your logging handlers to flush promptly - at minimum, flush on ERROR and above.
- Add a periodic heartbeat log line: it makes "silence" itself a detectable signal instead of an ambiguity between "healthy" and "buffered".

I created the DNS record for status.example.com 20 minutes ago. dig @1.1.1.1 returns the new A record, but dig @8.8.8.8 still returns NXDOMAIN. A monitoring probe had been querying the name since an hour before I created it. The SOA in the NXDOMAIN response shows a minimum TTL of 3600.

Nothing is wrong with your record - 8.8.8.8 is serving a cached *negative* answer. When the probe queried the name before it existed, resolvers cached the NXDOMAIN, and negative answers are cached for the zone's SOA minimum TTL - 3600 seconds here - counted from when each resolver asked, not from when you created the record. 1.1.1.1 either never cached the miss or had it expire, so it sees the truth already.

Fix: mostly patience - the stale NXDOMAIN expires within the hour. For faster convergence, both Google and Cloudflare offer public cache-flush pages for exactly this. And change the workflow that caused it: pre-create records before anything starts probing the name, because a pre-creation query is what poisons the cache. If you control the zone and do this often, a lower SOA negative TTL shortens the blast radius.

gRPC clients started failing after a proxy upgrade with errors like "error reading server preface" and "no application protocol". Running openssl s_client -alpn h2 -connect api.internal:443 now prints "No ALPN negotiated" - before the upgrade it printed "ALPN protocol: h2". The proxy config diff shows an alpn setting was removed from the listener.

You have the smoking gun already: ALPN is gone. gRPC runs over HTTP/2, and over TLS the two sides agree to speak HTTP/2 via ALPN during the handshake. With no ALPN negotiated, the client cannot confirm the server speaks h2 - strict clients abort ("no application protocol"), and ones that proceed anyway send an HTTP/2 preface to something that is not treating the connection as HTTP/2, producing the preface errors. The certificate, port, and backend are all fine; the handshake metadata changed under them.

Fix: restore ALPN on the listener (advertise h2, plus http/1.1 if the same endpoint serves REST), reload the proxy, and verify with the same s_client command - you want "ALPN protocol: h2" back. Then add ALPN to your synthetic monitoring of that endpoint: a check that only verifies "TLS connects and cert is valid" would have passed throughout this outage.

After migrating PostgreSQL to a new server, our daily reports shifted: date_trunc('day', created_at) now groups events differently - totals are off by a few hours around midnight versus the old reports. We verified the data is identical (created_at is timestamptz). On the new server, SHOW timezone returns UTC; the old server returned America/New_York.

The data did not change; the meaning of "day" did. timestamptz stores an absolute instant, but date_trunc and display convert it using the server's timezone setting. The old server truncated days at midnight New York time; the new one truncates at midnight UTC - a five-hour difference in where the boundary falls, which is exactly your symptom.

Fix, two options:
- Match the old semantics: ALTER DATABASE appdb SET timezone = 'America/New_York' (or set it for the reporting role), restoring the old grouping.
- Better, make reports explicit so a server setting can never silently redefine them again: date_trunc('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'). The AT TIME ZONE form pins the zone in the query itself.

Add "SHOW timezone" to your migration checklist - defaults like this (and encoding, and work_mem) are how migrations change behavior without changing data.

Our origin had a 3-minute outage an hour ago and recovered, but many users still see the error page. Response headers on the error page right now:

HTTP/2 500
cf-cache-status: HIT
age: 3421
cache-control: public, max-age=3600

The 500 response originally came from our app framework, which sends that Cache-Control header on all responses.

Your CDN cached the outage. During the 3-minute window, the origin's 500 response carried `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` (your framework sends it on *every* response, errors included), so the edge stored the error page as if it were good content for an hour. The Age: 3421 header - about 57 minutes - is the cached error's age, and cf-cache-status: HIT confirms users are being served the stored failure, not your recovered origin.

Fix now: purge the affected URLs at the CDN so the next request re-fetches from the healthy origin.
Fix permanently:
- At the origin, never send cacheable headers on 5xx: error responses should be `Cache-Control: no-store` (or private).
- At the CDN, set the error-caching TTL for 5xx to 0 or a few seconds regardless of origin headers - CDNs offer this precisely because origins mislabel errors.
Verify afterwards: Age resets and the status flips to MISS, then HIT on a 200.

Our rollback failed: the old binary exits at startup with "config version 7 not supported (max 6)". The bad deploy had migrated the on-disk config file in place from v6 to v7. There is no backup of the config - the deploy tool did not keep one.

The rollback unit was never just the binary. The deploy mutated shared state - the config file's format - and the old binary cannot read what the new one wrote, so "roll back the code" strands you with an unreadable config. This is the schema-migration problem one layer up, with the same moral.

Recover:
- Reconstruct a v6 config: the v7 file plus the release's config changelog usually lets you map fields back by hand (renames and additions are typically mechanical; drop v7-only keys, restore renamed ones). If the deploy tool supports a config downgrade command, use it - check before hand-editing.
- Start the old binary against the reconstructed config and verify it passes its own config validation.

Prevent: config migrations must (a) write a timestamped backup of the pre-migration file before touching it, (b) be listed in the rollback checklist alongside code and schema, and (c) ideally keep the old version readable for one release. A rollback plan that has not accounted for every artifact the deploy mutates - code, schema, config, cache keys - is a hope, not a plan.

PostgreSQL's disk hit 100%. The pg_wal directory is 300G. The log repeats, going back 9 days: "archive command failed with exit code 1" - the archive destination (a mounted archive volume) has been full/unreachable that whole time.

This is WAL doing exactly what it must, and the archiver failure is the incident. PostgreSQL cannot recycle or delete a WAL segment until it has been successfully archived. With archive_command failing, every segment is retained, so pg_wal grows at the database's full write rate until it takes the disk - and then the database itself stops, because it cannot write WAL either. Nine days of archive failures preceded the outage; the disk filling was the last step, not the first.

Fix:
1. Restore the archive path: free or repair the archive volume, or temporarily point archive_command at a healthy destination with enough room, then reload.
2. Let the archiver catch up - as segments archive successfully, pg_wal shrinks at the next checkpoints. Do NOT delete files from pg_wal by hand; removing segments the server still needs corrupts recovery.
3. Verify pg_wal is draining (watch its size and the archiver's success messages) before declaring victory.
4. Alert on archive_command failures themselves - one failure is a warning, and this must page long before day nine.

We scaled our app from 1 instance to 6, and now customers receive the 09:00 digest email six times. The logs on all six hosts show "digest job started" at 09:00:00. The scheduler is an in-process cron library inside the app.

An in-process scheduler runs once per *process*, not once per *system*. At one instance that distinction was invisible; at six instances you have six schedulers, all correctly firing the same 09:00 job - the six identical log lines are six instances each doing exactly what they were told. Nothing malfunctioned; the design assumed a singleton that no longer exists.

Fix, by increasing robustness:
- Simplest: run the digest from outside the app fleet - a single system cron, a Kubernetes CronJob, or one designated scheduler service.
- Or keep it in-process but elect a leader / take a lock: before working, each instance tries to insert a run row keyed by date into a table with a unique constraint (or grab an advisory lock); only the winner sends, the other five exit. This also protects you against double-fires from retries and clock oddities like the fall-back repeated hour.

Until one of those lands, the operational bandage is a config flag enabling the scheduler on exactly one instance - effective, but fragile if that instance is replaced.

One of the idle-in-transaction sessions has been open 2 hours (started by a reporting tool) and holds a lock on the orders table; 14 other sessions are waiting behind it. Our app servers keep timing out acquiring connections. What is wrong?

The 9 idle-in-transaction sessions are the problem, and one of them is the root of the timeouts. "Idle in transaction" means a session opened a transaction, ran something, and then went quiet *without committing or rolling back* - holding both its connection and its locks indefinitely. The 2-hour reporting-tool session holds a lock on orders that 14 other sessions are queued behind, and the queued sessions pin their own connections while they wait, which is why the app layer experiences it as connection starvation.

Fix now: terminate the blocking session (pg_terminate_backend) or have the reporting tool commit - the 14 waiters will drain immediately.
Fix permanently: set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (e.g. 60s) so abandoned transactions are rolled back automatically, and fix the reporting tool's pattern of opening a transaction and then pausing - a transaction should never span a human think-time or a slow export.

The team says "it will drain once the burst passes". Will it? If we want the backlog gone in 2 hours while producers keep running, what consumption rate do we need?

It will not drain - the team's premise is wrong. The queue is not draining slowly; it is *growing*: producers add 420/min against 270/min of consumption, a net +150/min, which matches the samples exactly (12,000 -> 15,200 in 20 minutes = +160/min, within measurement noise). A queue only drains when outflow exceeds inflow, and nothing here is a temporary "burst" - the rates are the steady state.

Alternatively pause producers and the current consumers clear it in 15,200 / 270 = ~56 minutes.

Summary of a thread dump from our app server (200 threads total) during a "the app is hung" incident:

state / top frame                              count
RUNNABLE                                       12
TIMED_WAITING (sleeping / backoff)             41
WAITING - HikariPool.getConnection (await)     147

The database itself is idle. Deadlock?

Not a deadlock - a queue. In a deadlock you would see threads BLOCKED on object monitors, and the dump would name a cycle of locks. Here 147 of 200 threads are parked in the connection pool's await, waiting to *borrow* a connection; only 12 are runnable. The application is not busy and not deadlocked - it is starved: every worker is queued for a resource the pool is not handing out, while the database sits idle (which fits: the connections are checked out and held somewhere, not actively querying).

So the investigation moves one layer down: who holds the pool's connections and why are they not coming back - leaked borrows, abandoned transactions, or a pool simply too small for a traffic step-change. The thread dump's job was to tell you where *not* to look: not CPU, not lock contention in your code, not the database's performance.

messages.name: database_query

The breakdown settles it: only 7 sessions are actually running queries, but 42 are *idle in transaction* - connections checked out by sessions that opened a transaction and then went quiet without committing. Those 42 are what saturate your pool: the database is idle while the pool is empty. Next step is to find the offenders (the same query with MIN(xact_start) grouped by application_name tells you which service and how old the oldest abandoned transaction is), then fix the code path that opens transactions across a wait, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as a safety net so abandoned transactions roll themselves back.
A cron entry `15 2 1 * 1` was supposed to run monthly on the 1st at 02:15. The team swears it also ran on Mondays in November 2026. Settle it: list every November 2026 date that entry fires.

The team is right: the entry fires 6 times in November 2026, not once. This is standard cron semantics - when both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, the job runs when *either* field matches (OR), not when both do. So `15 2 1 * 1` means 02:15 on the 1st of the month OR on every Monday: Nov 1 plus Nov 2, 9, 16, 23, 30. If you truly want "the 1st, only if it is also a Monday", cron cannot express AND directly - set one field to * and enforce the other condition inside the command with a date test.
